references.text: Jesus further explains by pointing to the woman as a daughter of Abraham whom Satan had bound for eighteen years—the context for why it is right to release her on the Sabbath, just as one unties an animal from its stall ([ref:Luk 13:16|Luke 13:16]).
Jesus uses a similar argument later: Which of you would not pull up his child or his ox that falls into a well on the Sabbath day? ([ref:Luk 14:5|Luke 14:5])
In Matthew, Jesus makes a comparable argument about pulling out a sheep that has fallen into a pit on the Sabbath to defend healing on the Sabbath ([ref:Matt 12:11|Matthew 12:11]).
Jesus calls the Pharisees and scribes "hypocrites" (ὑποκριταί), the same word he uses here to expose their double standard ([ref:Matt 23:13|Matthew 23:13]).

The Sabbath command in Deuteronomy requires rest also for oxen and donkeys, which presupposes that they must be cared for—namely, untied and given water, as Jesus argues ([ref:5 Mos 5:14|Deuteronomy 5:14]).
The purpose of the Sabbath includes rest for oxen and donkeys, showing that care for animals on the Sabbath is part of the law's intent ([ref:2 Mos 23:12|Exodus 23:12]).
Jesus asks whether it is lawful to do good or to do evil on the Sabbath—the overarching principle behind his defense of healing on the Sabbath ([ref:Luk 6:9|Luke 6:9]).

Jesus argues similarly in John: If a person can be circumcised on the Sabbath so that the Law of Moses is not broken, why are they angry because he healed a whole person on the Sabbath? ([ref:Joh 7:22-23|John 7:22-23])

Jesus calls the crowd hypocrites because they can interpret the signs of earth and sky but cannot interpret the signs of the times—a related use of "hypocrites" in the Gospel of Luke ([ref:Luk 12:56|Luke 12:56]).
